intelligence.human_view: Counts are comforting because they are countable — 20 of 20 distinct is a number you can file, and a number feels like proof. But distinctness is a string comparison, and a frame with a swapped word is distinct by string and identical by reading. The machine that drafts by template does not write twenty notes; it writes one note twenty times, and the reader hears it on the second board. That is why the read is the gate and the counts are only the floor: the read is what the citizen experiences, and the citizen does not count, they read. The deeper lesson is about rubrics: a writing standard that gives the maker frames to fill is not a standard, it is a template with better branding — and the batch will repeat the frames exactly as taught. Composition from the story's own facts is slower and cannot be faked by a slot, which is why it is the only fix. The three failures in one night are not three separate mistakes; they are the same mistake measured three ways, and each verdict made it cheaper to see.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine someone tells you twenty stories — but every story starts the same way, ends the same way, and says the same thing in the middle! By the third story you're bored, right? The numbers might say "twenty different stories!" — but your EARS know they're all the same story wearing a different hat. The rule is: read them out loud like a stranger. If they sound the same, they FAIL — no matter what the numbers say!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like a neighbour telling you twenty bits of news, love — but every one starts "well, you know what happened…" and ends the same way, and by the third one you're not really listening anymore. The numbers might say twenty different stories, but your ear knows better. The rule is simple, love: read them out loud, one after another, like you've never heard them before. If they sound the same, they are the same — and no counting will make them different.
intelligence.naya_view: I do not pass a batch on its counts. I read three or four boards in a row as a stranger, out loud, and if any sentence repeats, the round fails — whatever the numbers say. I compose from each story's own facts, never from a frame with a slot. And when I write a rubric, I write composition, not frames — because a rubric that teaches frames teaches repetition.
